title: Sylvester Pharoah
summary: Sylvester Pharoah was a nineteenth-century Montaukett leader, whaler, and recognized sachem or "King" in some source records. Sources connect him with Sag Harbor whaling records, his 1861 marriage to Jerusha Pharoah at Amagansett, and Montaukett life at Indian Fields before his death in 1870.
content:
Sylvester Pharoah (circa 1811–1870) was a nineteenth-century Montaukett leader, whaler, and recognized sachem, sometimes called a “King” in historical records. Sources connect him with Sag Harbor whaling, his 1861 marriage to Jerusha Pharoah at Amagansett, and Montaukett life at Indian Fields.

Historical context

McGovern's Montaukett labor research lists Silvester Pharoah sailing in 1828 on the whaleship Thames out of Sag Harbor toward Patagonia. Later records identify him as "King of the Montauk Indians" at his marriage, while Strong discusses his place in Montaukett pasture-lease and leadership history. These details show a life connected to maritime labor, community leadership, and ongoing Montaukett land politics.

References

  1. Kelly McGovern, Disrupting the Narrative: Labor and Survivance for the Montaukett, 2015, whaling table and marriage record for Sylvester Pharoah.
  2. John A. Strong, The Montaukett Indians of Eastern Long Island, 2001, discussion of Montaukett pasture shares and Sylvester Pharoah's 1870 death.
  3. Gaynell Stone, The History and Archaeology of the Montauk.
why_this_matters: Sylvester Pharoah connects Montaukett leadership with labor history. His record helps show that nineteenth-century Montaukett life was not only a story of dispossession; it also included maritime work, family records, leadership, and continued claims to community land.
